Overview
Marfan syndrome (Table 1)
Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder that affects elasticity and results in joint
laxity, scoliosis, cardiac valve changes, and aortic dilatation, among other problems. The
incidence is 1:10,000, with no ethnic or sex predilections.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS; Table 2)
EDS is a heterogenous group of heritable connective tissue disorders that affect collagen
production and metabolism
The most recent classification of EDS, which was published in 2017, includes 13 subtypes.
Each subtype is unique in its genetic basis, symptomatology, and diagnostic criteria.
In general, prominent features include joint hypermobility, skin hyperelasticity, and tissue
fragility.
Classic EDS and hypermobile EDS subtypes are commonly encountered in the clinical setting
and have autosomal dominant inheritance patterns.1

Etiology

Etiology
Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic mutation within the fibrillin-1 gene.
This is found on chromosome 15q21, and multiple mutations have been
identified. Twenty-five percent of diagnoses are new mutations.
The etiology of EDS is more complex because thirteen types have been identified.
Among patients with the classic form of EDS, 40% to 50% of have a mutation inCOL5A1 or
COL5A2, the genes for type V collagen; this classic form is autosomal dominant. The
other mutation that may result in classic EDS is in type I collagen, COL1A1, mutations in
which typically result in osteogenesis imperfecta. Kyphoscoliotic EDS (previously known
as type VI) is autosomal recessive and occurs secondary to a mutation in lysyl
hydroxylase, an enzyme important in collagen cross-linking. This type often manifests as
severe kyphoscoliosis. Vascular EDS is autosomal dominant and occurs secondary to a
mutation in COL3A1, resulting in abnormal type III collagen. Patients may have severe
complications with organ ruptures, including the intestines and uterus, and arterial
ruptures. Hypermobile EDS is the most common. Patients have joint hypermobility and
often have pain. Most patients do not have an identified mutation. These are the most
common of the thirteen recognized types of EDS.
Classification

Classification
The Ghent system for the diagnosis of Marfan syndrome requires one major criterion in
two different organ systems and involvement in a third system (Table 1). Patients with
the phenotype of mitral valve prolapse, aortic root diameter at upper limits of normal,
stretch marks, and skeletal manifestations of Marfan syndrome who do not have ectopia

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
5/20

lentis or aortic dissections have a better prognosis. The diagnosis of EDS is more
complex because of the multiple clinical manifestations and genetic variations (Table 2).
Mechanics of Fractures

Mechanics of Fractures
Patients with EDS and patients with Marfan syndrome are at risk for low bone density
and pathologic fractures. These usually begin around the teenage years and continue
into adulthood, with a high risk for early osteoporosis. The exact mechanism is unknown
but likely is related to the underlying collagen abnormalities.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
Marfan Syndrome
On physical examination, patients with Marfan syndrome will be tall and thin with long
limbs (dolichostenomelia), spiderlike fingers (arachnodactyly), and joint hypermobility.
The thumb and the little finger may overlap if used to encircle the opposite wrist
(Walker-Murdoch sign). Patients also may have a positive Steinberg sign, with the thumb
adducted across the palm and the fingers clenched into a fist across it, the tip of the
thumb protrudes past the lateral border of the hand. The ratio of arm span to height is
greater than 1.05.
Cardiac and ophthalmic findings are common in patients with Marfan syndrome. Heart
murmur or other abnormal findings may be present. Cardiac defects, especially aortic
root dilatation and later dissection are common. If Marfan syndrome is suspected,
echocardiography and a cardiology consultation are necessary. Superior lens dislocation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Connective Tissue Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
6/20

and myopia are common (rather than inferior lens dislocation, which is observed with
homocystinuria).
Musculoskeletal and chest wall differences are not uncommon in patients with Marfan
syndrome. Scoliosis is observed in 60% to 70% of patients and is difficult to brace; dural
ectasia is common (>60% of patients), necessitating preoperative MRI(Figure 1). Pectus
excavatum and spontaneous pneumothoraces may occur in the chest (Figure 2).
Protrusio acetabuli and severe pes planovalgus are observed in the lower extremities.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
Physical examination my reveal fragile and velvety skin in patients with classic types of EDS, with
the potential for severe scarring with even minor trauma; however, this is not present with all
phenotypes. Joints, particularly the shoulders, patellae, and ankles, are hypermobile. As many as
one-third of patients with EDS have aortic root dilatations; therefore, echocardiography and a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Connective Tissue Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
8/20

cardiac evaluation are mandatory. The vascular subtype may result in spontaneous visceral or
arterial ruptures.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques and Procedures

Techniques and Procedures
Nonsurgical management of Marfan syndrome consists of a multidisciplinary approach
involving pediatricians, cardiologiests, ophthalmologists, orthopaedics surgeons, and
other medical professionals. Mitral valve prolapse and aortic dilation should be
appropriately managed via beta-blockers. Routine monitoring via echocardiography is
mandatory. Regular eye examinations also are recommended. Brace management can
be used to manage the most common orthopaedic problems, which include scoliosis
and pes planovalgus.
Joint laxity and pain in patients with EDS initially should be managed via physical therapy
regimens that focus on strengthening and stabilization. Chronic musculoskeletal pain is
present in more than 50% of patients; this should be managed supportively if possible.
Many patients will benefit from the involvement of a pain management physician/team.
Surgical Management
Techniques and Procedures

Techniques and Procedures
Common surgical indications for Marfan syndrome include scoliosis and pes
planovalgus, with a slightly less common indication being progressive protrusio
acetabuli. Spinal fusion for scoliosis often necessitates fusion of additional levels
secondary to problems with junctional kyphosis. Preoperative workup for scoliosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Connective Tissue Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
9/20

surgery includes MRI (to assess dural ectasia) and a cardiac workup. Surgeons should be
aware of higher pseudarthrosis and revision rates in patients with Marfan scoliosis.
Corrective surgical procedures for pes planovalgus are made on a case-by-case basis.
Patients with progressive potrusion acetabuli may be candidates for closure of the
triradiate cartilage.
Scoliosis is most common in patients with type VI EDS and usually is progressive. Surgical
management is indicated for progressive curves, and longer fusions are necessary to
prevent junctional problems (Figure 3).

Rheumatoid (seropositive) arthritis (Table 3)

Seronegative spondyloarthropathies 

Overview
Osteoarthritis is the classic arthritis of older age, caused by “wear and tear”. The other
types of arthritis discussed in this lesson are inflammatory autoimmune types of
arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis results in joint destruction at a younger age. Rheumatoid
arthritis is separate from JIA (not classified as rheumatoid arthritis), which is arthritis of
the joints in children that lasts for more than 6 weeks. Seronegative
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Connective Tissue Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
12/20

spondyloarthropathies also exist. Although, caused by autoimmune etiologies, patients
with seronegative spondyloarthropathies do not test positive for rheumatoid factor.
Epidemiology
Rheumatoid (seropositive) arthritis
JIA
Systemic JIA (Still disease)
Oligarticular JIA (pauciarticular JRA)
Polyarticular JIA (polyarticuluar JRA)
Ankylosing spondylitis

Epidemiology
Rheumatoid factor is noted in only one-half of patients with rheumatoid arthritis and in
5% of the general population; however, it may help identify more aggressive cases. The
prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis is 1% in the general population; prevalence is higher
in aboriginal North Americans. Twin concordance is only 12% to 15% for monozygotic
twins, suggesting that a genetic etiology, although present, is not the only cause of
rheumatoid arthritis.
Systemic JIA, usually is observed in children aged 5 to 10 years and affects girls and boys
equally. Systemic disease is associated with a poorer long-term prognosis; however, it is
the least common type of JIA, affecting only 20% of patients. Oligoarticular JIA is
associated with a peak age of 2 to 3 years and is four times more common in girls than in
boys. Of all the types of JIA, oligoarticular JIA is associated with the best prognosis for
long-term remission (70%). Polyarticular JIA is more common in girls than in boys. The
prognosis for patients with polyarticular JIA is particularly good (60% remission). Among
the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, ankylosing spondylitis most commonly affects
patients aged 15 to 35 years and affects males more than females. Symptoms are
characterized by morning stiffness and low back pain.

Etiology
Osteoarthritis
Rheumatoid (seropositive) arthritis
JIA
Seronegative spondyloarthropathies
Ankylosing spondylitis
Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome)

Etiology
Osteoarthritis is caused by mechanical forces. Varus or valgus malalignment of more
than 4° to 5° in the knee yields a fourfold increase in knee osteoarthritis. Overuse or
joint incongruity or injury damages chondrocytes, leading to cartilage breakdown in the
joint.
In patients with seropositive arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis and JIA), the synovium
thickens and fills with B and T cells and macrophages, which erode the cartilage. This is
an autoimmune systemic process. In patients with JIA, the process can be systemic or
only occur in certain joints. A positive rheumatoid factor and an antinuclear antibody
(ANA) may indicate an aggressive course.
Similarly, the seronegative spondyloarthropathies also are autoimmune in nature. For
ankylosing spondylitis, 95% of White patients and 50% of Black patients with ankylosing
spondylitis are human leukocyte antigen–B27 positive; however, less than 5% of all
individuals who are human leukocyte antigen–B27 positive have ankylosing spondylitis.
Reactive arthritis is triggered by diseases, such as Chlamydia, Yersinia, Salmonella,
Campylobacter, or Shigella infections, that lead to an autoimmune complex deposition in
the joints (commonly the knee).
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Physical Examination

Rheumatoid (seropositive) arthritis
Physical examination reveals multiple hot, swollen, stiff joints.
JIA
Systemic JIA (Still disease)
Rash, high fever, multiple inflamed joints, and acute presentation are typical.

(commonly the knee), which leads to painful swelling.
Enteropathic arthropathies

Physical Examination
Physical examination for osteoarthritis reveals joint stiffness, typically in the
interphalangeal joints of the hands, hips, and knees, without signs of acute systemic
inflammation. With rheumatoid arthritis, physical examination reveals multiple hot,
swollen, stiff joints, which is evidence of inflammation. Subcutaneous calcified nodules
and iridis may be present.
Patients with systemic JIA (Still disease) have a rash, high fever, and multiple inflamed
joints. Often, presentation is acute in patients with systemic JIA compared with the more
insidious presentation of the types of arthritis already mentioned. Anemia and/or a high
white blood cell count may be noted. Patients may have serositis, hepatosplenomegaly,
lymphadenopathy, or pericarditis. Infection must be ruled out in patients with these
findings. Physical examination of patients with oligoarticulaur JIA reveals four or fewer
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Connective Tissue Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
15/20

involved joints. Usually the large joints, commonly the knees and ankles, are affected. A
limp that improves during the day is typical. Uveitis occurs in 20% of patients. An
ophthalmology evaluation is necessary every 4 months in patients who are ANA positive
and every 6 months in patients who are ANA negative. Limb-length discrepancy, with the
affected side often longer, is another sequela. Polyarticular JIA is diagnosed if five or
more joints are involved, and often small joints (hands and wrists) are affected. Patients
may have uveitis; however, it is less frequent than in patients with oligoarticular JIA.
With ankylosing spondylitis, sacroiliitis and progressive fusion of the spine (bamboo
spine) are typical. Peripheral joint arthritis, usually unilateral, is common. Uveitis is
present in as many as 40% of patients; cardiac and pulmonary disease also can occur.
Aphthous mouth ulcers and fatigue are common.
In patients with psoriatic arthritis, the typical psoriatic skin plaques (extensor surface
scaly silvery plaques) usually precede arthritis; however, arthritis occurs first in 20% of
patients. A common radiographic finding is pencil-in-cup deformities of the phalanges.
Nail pitting and dactylitis commonly are observed. Reactive arthritis consists of painful
swelling after an infection of a joint (typically a knee). Reactive arthritis is associated with
conjunctivitis and dysuria. Mouth ulcers and a rash on the hands and feet also can occur.
Enteropathic arthropathies occur in 20% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease,
such as Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis. These patients have joint pain and swelling in
addition to gastrointestinal symptoms.

Radiographic findings of rheumatoid arthritis include symmetric joint space narrowing,
periarticular erosions, and osteopenia. Radiographic findings of ankylosing spondylitis
includede erosions and sclerosis in the sacroiliac joints, with eventual widening of the
joint space and bony sclerosis. This leads to the bamboo spine appearance.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques and Procedures
Osteoarthritis
Management is supportive
Rheumatoid (seropositive) arthritis
Currently, rheumatoid arthritis is mostly managed medically.
JIA
In general, medical management via NSAIDs or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs by
a rheumatologist generally is required.
Ankylosing spondylitis
Currently, ankylosing spondylitis is primarily managed medically.
Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome)
Manage the underlying condition and manage the arthritis supportively.
Enteropathic arthropathies
Manage the underlying condition, and manage the arthritis supportively.

Techniques and Procedures
For osteoarthritis, management mostly is supportive with physical therapy and NSAIDs
and/or cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors used first, and osteotomy and joint replacement
reserved for patients in the later stages of the disease process. Currently, cartilage
replacement via techniques such as mosaicplasty and autologous chondrocyte
implantation is limited. Genetically engineered cartilage regrowth is a future treatment
option. Rheumatoid arthritis management largely is medical via a combination of NSAIDs
and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. In general, a rheumatologist is required to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Connective Tissue Diseases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003011
17/20

manage these medications. Most disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are
immunosuppressive and must be stopped before orthopaedic procedures, with cell
count evaluated to avoid neutropenia.
JIA requires medical management via NSAIDs or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs
by a rheumatologist. For ankylosing spondylitis, aggressive physical therapy and NSAIDs
are indicated. Spinal fractures are highly unstable and associated with a high rate of
neurologic injury. For reactive arthritis and enteropathic arthritis, the first goal is to
manage the underlying condition (infection, inflammatory bowel disease), after which
the arthritis can be managed supportively.
Surgical Management
Techniques and Procedures
Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid (seropositive) arthritis
Surgical management involves synovectomy and joint realignment early on and joint
replacement in the later stages of the disease process.
JIA
Steroid injections and synovectomy may be helpful if medical management fails.

Techniques and Procedures
For osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, joint replacement is an option for patients in
later stages of the disease process. Some patients with rheumatoid arthritis also benefit
from synovectomy and joint realignment early in the disease process.
For patients with JIA, leg-length discrepancy may require epiphysiodesis. Arthroplasty
may be necessary in adults. Steroid injections and synovectomy may be helpful if
medical management fails.
